title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Runbooks
author: Avery Chen
summary: Consolidated reference for the Redwood serving runtime: architecture overview, kernel scheduling strategies, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks. This page is the canonical starting point for engineers onboarding to the runtime and for on-call responders.
body:
Overview

This document consolidates operational and engineering guidance for Redwood's GPU-optimized serving runtime. It covers: runtime architecture, kernel scheduling strategies and tunables, profiling playbooks for performance investigations, the benchmarking suite and expected results, release notes for recent runtime versions, an up-to-date known-issues list with mitigations, and runbooks used by on-call and SRE teams.

Table of contents
1. Runtime architecture overview
2. Kernel scheduling design and configuration
3. Profiling playbook (how-to)
4. Benchmarking suite and expected metrics
5. Release notes (recent)
6. Known issues and mitigations
7. Runtime runbooks (on-call)
8. Team wiki, ownership, and links
9. Appendix: configs and CLI examples

1) Runtime architecture overview

Intro
The serving runtime provides a high-throughput, low-latency inference engine. Primary goals: predictable latency (P95/SLO targets), high GPU utilization for cost efficiency, and graceful degradation across capacity tiers. The runtime is implemented as a microservice suite with clear separation of responsibilities.

Core components (logical)
- Ingress / API Gateway: handles auth, rate limits, and initial request shaping.
- Request Router: decides model variant, region, and fallback policy.
- Scheduler / Worker Pool: assigns work to GPU workers with batching and priority lanes.
- Inference Engine (GPU worker): model execution, KV cache access, quantized kernels.
- Cache Service: prefix and KV cache with LRU+TTL policies.
- Telemetry & Tracing: structured metrics, tracing hooks, per-request cost estimation.
- Orchestration: autoscaling controller and placement driver for Dedicated pools.

Deployment topology (textual diagram)
- Edge -> API Gateway -> Router -> Scheduler -> Worker Pool (GPU nodes) -> Storage/Cache
- Control plane runs separately and manages model versions, rollouts, and policies.

SLOs and targets (examples)
- Text generation P95 latency (short prompts, 256 tokens): <= 120ms (hosted tiers)
- Text generation P99 latency (short prompts): <= 350ms
- Worker GPU utilization target: 60-80% under steady-state batchable workloads
- Error budget: 99.9% success rate per release window

Ownership and directories
- Primary owners: serving-runtime team (eng-serving-runtime).
- Observability dashboards: Grafana -> /dashboards/serving-runtime/main
- Benchmark results: artifact storage -> s3://redwood-ci/benchmarks/serving-runtime/

2) Kernel scheduling design and configuration

Design goals
- Maximize throughput while meeting latency SLOs.
- Prefer batching compatible requests, but protect low-latency flows with priority lanes.
- Support heterogeneous GPU types and quantization profiles.

Scheduler types
- Latency-first scheduler: small batches, strict P95 budgets (used for hosted low-latency tier).
- Throughput-first scheduler: larger batches, higher GPU packing (used for background/cheap tiers).
- Hybrid scheduler: dynamic batching with fairness and response-time budgets.

Key tunables (config table)
| Parameter | Description | Typical values |
|-----------|-------------|----------------|
| max_batch_size | Maximum tokens per batch | 64 / 128 / 512 |
| batch_timeout_ms | How long to wait to fill a batch | 5 / 10 / 30 |
| priority_lanes | Number of reserved lanes for high-priority requests | 1-3 |
| kv_cache_ttl_ms | Time to keep KV cache entries | 60000 |
| preemptive_yield_threshold | GPU kernel time (ms) to allow preemption | 5-50 |

Configuration example (YAML snippet)
scheduler:
  policy: hybrid
  max_batch_size: 128
  batch_timeout_ms: 10
  priority_lanes: 2
  preemptive_yield_threshold: 20

Best practices
- Use smaller max_batch_size for short-sequence conversational workloads.
- Tune batch_timeout_ms per region/latency profile; prefer < 20ms for low-latency tiers.
- Monitor fairness metrics (latency delta across customers) when enabling throughput-first policies.

3) Profiling playbook (how-to)

When to run this playbook
- High P95/P99 regressions after a release.
- Unexplained GPU under-utilization or sudden latency spikes.
- Degraded tail latency for a subset of customers or routes.

Prerequisites (tools + permissions)
- Access to Grafana dashboards and traces.
- SSH / bastion access to worker node (owner permission).
- Profiling tools: nvprof / Nsight Systems / CUPTI traces, nvtop, perf, pmap, python cProfile for orchestration code.
- A reproducible request workload: locally recorded scenario or replay harness.

Step-by-step profiling flow
1. Confirm symptom windows in observability: check P50/P95/P99, request rate, queue lengths.
2. Isolate an affected worker node (use routing rules) or reproduce locally with the same model + quantization.
3. Collect high-level metrics (5-10 minutes): nvidia-smi, nvtop, GPU mem, rpc queue depth.
4. Run a lightweight Nsight Systems trace for a single request to capture kernel launches and CPU blocking: nsight-sys -o trace.qdrep --target-processes all --duration 30s.
5. If kernel inefficiency suspected, collect CUPTI traces and symbolized kernels.
6. Capture scheduler-level traces: batch formation times, enqueue/dequeue latencies, preemption events.
7. Correlate with KV cache hit-rate and model variance.
8. Produce a short report with: root cause hypothesis, evidence (screenshots/links to traces), proposed fix, and a rollback plan if the fix is risky.

Checklist of metrics to capture
- Kernel execution time distribution (ms)
- Kernel launch overhead (ms)
- Batch formation time (ms)
- GPU occupancy and SM utilization (%)
- PCIe transfer time (ms) and size (MB)
- Host-side queue latency (ms)
- KV cache hit-rate (%)

Common findings and mitigations
- Symptom: long host-side batching delays -> Cause: small batch_timeout_ms or skewed request arrival -> Mitigation: increase batch_timeout_ms for non-latency-critical lanes; add adaptive batching.
- Symptom: low SM utilization with many small kernels -> Cause: kernel fragmentation due to quantization or async dispatch -> Mitigation: use fused kernels, increase kernel grouping, or upgrade kernel binaries.
- Symptom: high PCIe transfer time -> Cause: frequent model swaps or large KV fills -> Mitigation: pin models to GPU memory, reduce model warmups, or use NVLink when possible.

4) Benchmarking suite and expected metrics

Purpose
- Provide a reproducible harness for performance regressions, capacity planning, and relative comparisons between kernel releases and quantization profiles.

Benchmark components
- Workload generator: supports chat, single-turn generation, embeddings, and reranking. Uses recorded latency distributions.
- Config profiles: small_prompt, conversational, long_generation, batchable_inference.
- Metrics collector: Prometheus snapshots + artifactized tracer output.

Example benchmark config (JSON)
{
  "profile": "conversational",
  "qps": "100",
  "avg_prompt_tokens": "32",
  "target_seq": "128",
  "duration_min": "20"
}

Key metrics collected
- Mean / P50 / P95 / P99 latency (ms)
- Tokens-per-second (aggregate)
- GPU utilization and average batch size
- Cost estimate (tokens * cost-per-token model)

Acceptable baselines (example for v1.12 kernels)
- conversational@100qps: P95 <= 120ms, tokens/sec >= 12000, GPU util 65%
- long_generation@20qps: P95 <= 400ms, tokens/sec >= 6000, GPU util 60%

Running a benchmark
1. Checkout benchmark harness: git@github.com:redwood/serving-benchmarks.git (branch main).
2. Configure target cluster and credentials.
3. Run: ./bench/run.sh --config configs/conversational-100qps.json --artifact-dir /tmp/bench-$(date +%F)
4. Upload artifacts: aws s3 cp /tmp/bench-... s3://redwood-ci/benchmarks/<run-id>/ --recursive
5. Link results in PRs or release notes.

5) Release notes (recent)

v2026.05.25 - Runtime kernel release (v1.12):
- Improved fused attention kernel for Llama-style models (avg kernel time -18%).
- New scheduler hybrid policy (hybrid-v2) with dynamic batch-time adaptation.
- Bug fix: prevented KV cache eviction on short rolling restarts.
- Known impact: some TPUs/third-party kernels report higher host-launch overhead; see Known Issues section.

v2026.04.10 - Runtime patch (v1.11.3):
- Fix: off-by-one in batch accounting that could cause occasional OOMs under heavy batching.
- Telemetry: added per-kernel histograms to Prometheus.

Compatibility notes
- When upgrading kernel libraries, verify quantization profiles and model transforms; older quantized model artifacts may require re-quantization.

6) Known issues and mitigations

1. High host-kernel launch latency on some A100 machines (ticket: RW-4532)
- Symptom: elevated kernel-launch ms and P99 latency for small-batch workloads.
- Workaround: pin model memory, set preemptive_yield_threshold to 40ms, and enable fused-kernel path.
- Target fix: kernel driver update and redesigned batching glue (ETA next quarter).

2. Occasional KV cache corruption after A/B rollout (ticket: RW-4678)
- Symptom: cache misses and small incorrect entries after simultaneous rollouts on a node.
- Mitigation: force KV cache warmup on first request after rollout and monitor cache CRCs; rollback if CRC mismatch rate > 0.1%.

3. Transient OOMs under mixed workloads (ticket: RW-4387)
- Symptom: worker OOM during high concurrent long-generation jobs.
- Mitigation: enable per-tenant memory quotas and soft-eviction; reduce max_batch_size for long_generation profile.

7) Runtime runbooks (on-call)

Primary alerting channels
- PagerDuty: "serving-runtime-p1" (critical, P95/P99 outages)
- Slack: #serving-runtime-ops (paged for P2 incidents)

Incident triage (short)
1. Acknowledge the alert and capture window.
2. Check dashboard: API gateway error rate, router queue depth, scheduler queue lengths, worker node health.
3. If errors are gateway/auth related, escalate to eng-platform.
4. If queue depth high with healthy workers -> investigate scheduler config or slow kernels.
5. If a subset of nodes show high error rates -> isolate nodes and drain traffic.
6. For OOMs: check GC/memory metrics, recent deploys, and revert if necessary.

Example runbook entries (table)
| Symptom | Initial checks | Immediate mitigation | Owner |
|---------|----------------|----------------------|-------|
| P99 spike across all regions | Check routing, rate limiter, infra | Throttle non-critical routes, enable canary fallback | serving-runtime on-call |
| Worker OOMs | Inspect dmesg, container logs, recent deploy | Drain node, restart worker, rollback last deploy | infra-sre |
| High kernel latency | Collect Nsight trace, check GPU metrics | Switch to fused-kernel fallback, increase batch_timeout | serving-runtime eng |

Post-incident
- Create incident summary in /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems and tag this doc.
- Link traces and benchmarks to the incident record.

8) Team wiki, ownership, and links

Where to look

- Runbooks directory: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks
- Benchmarks artifacts: s3://redwood-ci/benchmarks/serving-runtime/

Rotations and contacts
- Serving runtime on-call: rotation managed in PagerDuty; primary contact is the weekly on-call engineer.
- Owners: Avery Chen (runtime architecture), Marcus Patel (scheduling & kernels), Elena Novak (benchmarks & profiling).

Contributing
- To propose changes to scheduler defaults or kernel builds: open a PR in repo infra/serving-runtime-config and reference this doc. Include benchmark results showing delta vs baseline.

9) Appendix: configs and CLI examples

Scheduler inspection commands
- Show scheduler queues: curl -s http://<worker>:9090/debug/scheduler | jq .queue_stats
- Dump current scheduler config: curl -s http://<control-plane>/v1/scheduler/config | jq .

Profiling quick commands
- Lightweight GPU usage: watch -n 1 nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,memory.used --format=csv
- Nsight trace (30s): nsight-sys -o /tmp/trace.qdrep --target-processes all --duration 30s --capture-range full

Benchmark run example
- ./bench/run.sh --config configs/conversational-100qps.json --target-cluster prod-dedicated --artifact-dir /tmp/bench-run

Contact and escalation
- For critical incidents: PagerDuty "serving-runtime-p1" -> follow incident triage.
- Non-critical engineering questions: Slack #serving-runtime-dev.
